math_plain: Learns to split documents into semantic chunks by optimizing whether resulting chunks align with question intent, rewarding chunks that preserve logical coherence and context.
why_math: It works because questions reveal what information patterns matter; chunks that answer questions together naturally preserve meaning, whereas arbitrary splits fragment knowledge—questions act as ground truth for correct semantic boundaries.

math_plain: Prunes network capacity while carefully preserving the ability to learn new tasks by expanding capacity temporarily at task boundaries then re-pruning.
why_math: It works because the capacity to adapt depends on having room to store new patterns; by expanding at critical moments when learning new material and re-pruning afterward, the model keeps only essential connections while staying flexible enough to absorb new knowledge.

why_math: It works because real opinion dynamics depend on how fast emotions fade versus how persistent beliefs are; modeling both mechanisms separately then letting them interact produces trajectories that match actual data because it captures the dual-speed nature of how humans actually change their minds.

why_math: It works because addiction follows economic principles—people trade off short-term reward against long-term cost—and behavioral data encodes these tradeoffs implicitly; weighting by individual differences captures why some users escalate while others self-regulate.

why_math: It works because identical input sets applied to both versions reveal the boundaries of their differences; inputs that split behavior pinpoint exactly which edge cases expose the bug, eliminating false leads and showing the true source of failure.

why_math: It works because conflicting values in raw data force models to compromise; filtering for data where values align smoothly creates cleaner learning signals, then linearly blending these smooth models preserves all their learned trade-offs without the noise that destroys alignment.

why_math: It works because real temporal dynamics operate at multiple speeds—some changes happen fast (hours), others slow (months)—and wavelets naturally separate these scales; tracking both simultaneously gives a complete picture of what's likely to happen next in the network.
